t: Number of Subarrays Having Even Product
o: A subarray's product is even iff it contains at least one even number. Total subarrays = n(n+1)/2; subtract those with all-odd elements. Efficient one-pass: keep lastEven = index of the most recent even number; the number of subarrays ending at i with even product equals lastEven + 1 (all starts ≤ lastEven include that even element). Sum these. Example 1: evens at index 1 → contributions 0,1,2,3 → wait: at i=0 lastEven=-1→0; i=1 lastEven=1→2; i=2→3; i=3→4; total 6 ✓. Example 2: no evens → 0 ✓.
k: Even product ⟺ subarray contains an even element.
Subarrays ending at i with even product = (index of last even ≤ i) + 1.
Equivalently: total − (count of all-odd subarrays via consecutive-odd runs).

a.i: Count maximal runs of consecutive odd numbers; a run of length L contributes L(L+1)/2 all-odd subarrays. Subtract from n(n+1)/2.
s: Walk the array, tracking current run length of odds.
On an even number, add run*(run+1)/2 to oddCount and reset run = 0.
Answer = n(n+1)/2 − oddCount (flush the final run).

a.i: For each right endpoint i, the count of valid subarrays ending at i is (lastEvenIndex + 1). One pass, direct accumulation, no subtraction needed.
s: For each i: if nums[i] even, last = i; add last + 1 to answer.

w: Use 64-bit accumulation: n = 1e5 gives ~5e9 subarrays, overflowing 32-bit ints. Both approaches are O(n); the last-even method generalizes better (e.g., 'subarrays divisible by 2^j'). Pitfall: parity check with % on positives is fine here since nums[i] ≥ 1. Follow-up: count subarrays with odd product only (just the run-counting part), or products divisible by 6.
